summary:
Condition factor (K) compares a fish's weight with the weight you would expect for its length. It returns condition factor (K), expected weight at K = 1, weight against K = 1 and fish weight, and the panel shows all of them at once.

It is the standard way to describe how well-fed, how healthy or how well-shaped a fish is, and it is used in fisheries assessment, aquaculture and aquarium husbandry. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Fish Condition Factor
sections.html:
K = (weight in grams ÷ fork length in cm³) × 100

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
weighttotal body weightg
lengthfork lengthcm
kFulton's condition factor—

Where the relationship comes from. Fulton (1904) condition factor; ranges follow standard fisheries assessment practice.

sections.title: How do I use the Fish Condition Factor?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
Interpretation is a convention, not part of the arithmetic. The usual bands are:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
below 1.0Poor conditionthin fish; check feeding, disease and water quality
1.0 – 1.4Normalthe usual range for most species
above 1.4Excellentwell fed, often pre-spawning or a deep-bodied species

  • Fulton's K assumes the fish grows isometrically (weight ∝ length³). For species that change shape as they grow, the relative condition factor against a species-specific regression is the better measure.

  • K rises before spawning in females and falls after it, so single measurements taken at different times of year are not comparable.

  • A K below 1.0 in a well-fed tank usually means a water-quality or parasite problem, not underfeeding.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Using total length in one measurement and fork length in another — the difference is several per cent of length and 10% or more of K.
  • Weighing a wet fish with a wet net, or a gutted fish, without saying so.
  • Comparing K across species as if 1.0 meant the same thing everywhere.

faq.q: What is a good condition factor for a fish?
faq.a: Around 1.0–1.4 for most freshwater species; below 1.0 suggests the fish is thin for its length and above 1.4 that it is in good condition — but the normal band is species-specific.

faq.q: Should I use fork length or total length?
faq.a: Whatever you use, use it consistently and say which. This calculator is set up for fork length, which is standard in fisheries work.

faq.q: What does the Fish Condition Factor actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns condition factor (K), expected weight at K = 1, weight against K = 1 and fish weight. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
